claim: BIRDS is an open-source software for mapping and analysis of 3D microscopy data applied to the mouse brain.
source: We have developed an open-source software called bi-channel image registration and deep-learning segmentation (BIRDS) for the mapping and analysis of 3D microscopy data and applied this to the mouse brain.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as the main contribution of the work.

claim: The BIRDS pipeline includes image preprocessing, bi-channel registration, automatic annotation, creation of a 3D digital frame, high-resolution visualization, and expandable quantitative analysis.
source: The BIRDS pipeline includes image preprocessing, bi-channel registration, automatic annotation, creation of a 3D digital frame, high-resolution visualization, and expandable quantitative analysis.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract describing the components of the pipeline.

claim: The bi-channel registration algorithm is adaptive to various types of whole-brain data from different microscopy platforms.
source: This new bi-channel registration algorithm is adaptive to various types of whole-brain data from different microscopy platforms and shows dramatically improved registration accuracy.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a key feature of the algorithm.

claim: The bi-channel registration algorithm shows dramatically improved registration accuracy.
source: This new bi-channel registration algorithm is adaptive to various types of whole-brain data from different microscopy platforms and shows dramatically improved registration accuracy.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by comparative data in Figure 2.

claim: The registration procedure can readily provide training data for network construction.
source: Additionally, as this platform combines registration with neural networks, its improved function relative to the other platforms lies in the fact that the registration procedure can readily provide training data for network construction, while the trained neural network can efficiently segment-incomplete/defective brain data that is otherwise difficult to register.
evidence: Stated in the abstract describing the synergistic relationship between registration and neural networks.

claim: The trained neural network can efficiently segment incomplete/defective brain data that is otherwise difficult to register.
source: Additionally, as this platform combines registration with neural networks, its improved function relative to the other platforms lies in the fact that the registration procedure can readily provide training data for network construction, while the trained neural network can efficiently segment-incomplete/defective brain data that is otherwise difficult to register.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: BIRDS enables minute-timescale registration-based segmentation of cross-modality, whole-brain datasets.
source: Our software is thus optimized to enable either minute-timescale registration-based segmentation of cross-modality, whole-brain datasets or real-time inference-based image segmentation of various brain regions of interest.
evidence: Stated in the abstract describing the performance capabilities.

claim: BIRDS enables real-time inference-based image segmentation of various brain regions of interest.
source: Our software is thus optimized to enable either minute-timescale registration-based segmentation of cross-modality, whole-brain datasets or real-time inference-based image segmentation of various brain regions of interest.
evidence: Stated in the abstract describing the performance capabilities.

claim: BIRDS is implemented as a Fiji plugin that can be adapted to most computing environments.
source: Jobs can be easily submitted and implemented via a Fiji plugin that can be adapted to most computing environments.
evidence: Stated in the abstract describing the software implementation.

claim: The Mouse Brain Architecture project has mapped the mouse brain in terms of cell types, long-range connectivity patterns, and microcircuit connectivity.
source: Large projects, including the Mouse Brain Architecture project (Bohland et al., 2009), the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (Oh et al., 2014), and the Mouse Connectome project, have mapped the mouse brain (Zingg et al., 2014) in terms of cell types, long-range connectivity patterns, and microcircuit connectivity.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas has mapped the mouse brain in terms of cell types, long-range connectivity patterns, and microcircuit connectivity.
source: Large projects, including the Mouse Brain Architecture project (Bohland et al., 2009), the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (Oh et al., 2014), and the Mouse Connectome project, have mapped the mouse brain (Zingg et al., 2014) in terms of cell types, long-range connectivity patterns, and microcircuit connectivity.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The Mouse Connectome project has mapped the mouse brain in terms of cell types, long-range connectivity patterns, and microcircuit connectivity.
source: Large projects, including the Mouse Brain Architecture project (Bohland et al., 2009), the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (Oh et al., 2014), and the Mouse Connectome project, have mapped the mouse brain (Zingg et al., 2014) in terms of cell types, long-range connectivity patterns, and microcircuit connectivity.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: An increasing number of laboratories are developing independent, automated, or semi-automated frameworks for processing brain data obtained for specific projects.
source: In addition to these large-scale collaborative efforts, an increasing number of laboratories are also developing independent, automated, or semi-automated frameworks for processing brain data obtained for specific projects (Fürth et al., 2018; Ni et al., 2020; Niedworok et al., 2016; Renier et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020a; Iqbal et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Development of a standardized and automated computational pipeline to map, analyze, visualize, and share brain data has become a major challenge to all brain connectivity mapping efforts.
source: With the improvement of experimental methods for dissection of brain connectivity and function, development of a standardized and automated computational pipeline to map, analyze, visualize, and share brain data has become a major challenge to all brain connectivity mapping efforts (Alivisatos et al., 2012; Fürth et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The commonly used approach for automatic anatomical segmentation is to register an experimental image dataset within a standardized, fully segmented reference space.
source: The commonly used approach for automatic anatomical segmentation is to register an experimental image dataset within a standardized, fully segmented reference space, thus obtaining the anatomical segmentation for this set of experimental images (Oh et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2020; Renier et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Most registration-based frameworks require the user to set a few parameters based on the image intensity or graphics outlines or to completely convert the dataset into a framework-readable format to ensure the quality of the resulting segmentation.
source: Most of these frameworks require the user to set a few parameters based on the image intensity or graphics outlines or to completely convert the dataset into a framework-readable format to ensure the quality of the resulting segmentation.
evidence: Stated in the introduction describing limitations of existing frameworks.

claim: The heterogeneous and non-uniform characteristics of brain structures make it difficult to use traditional registration methods for registering datasets from different imaging platforms to a standard brain space with high accuracy.
source: However, with the rapid development of sample labeling technology (Lee et al., 2016; Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Schwarz et al., 2015) and high-resolution whole-brain microscopic imaging (Economo et al., 2016; Gong et al., 2013; Nie et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010), the heterogeneous and non-uniform characteristics of brain structures make it difficult to use traditional registration methods for registering datasets from different imaging platforms to a standard brain space with high accuracy.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Laborious visual inspection, followed by manual correction, is often required for traditional registration methods, which significantly reduces the productivity of these techniques.
source: In this case, laborious visual inspection, followed by manual correction, is often required, which significantly reduces the productivity of these techniques.
evidence: Stated in the introduction describing limitations of existing methods.

claim: Registration-based methods lack the flexibility to analyze incomplete brain datasets or those focused on a certain volume of interest.
source: Moreover, though registration-based methods can achieve full anatomical annotation in reference to a standard atlas for whole-brain datasets, their region-based 3D registration to a whole-brain atlas lacks the flexibility to analyze incomplete brain datasets or those focused on a certain volume of interest (Song and Song, 2018), which is often the case in neuroscience research.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation supporting the claim.

claim: Some frameworks can register certain types of brain slabs that contain complete coronal outlines slice by slice.
source: Though some frameworks can register certain types of brain slabs that contain complete coronal outlines slice by slice (Fürth et al., 2018; Song and Song, 2018; Ferrante and Paragios, 2017), it remains very difficult to register a small brain block without obvious anatomical outlines.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: It remains very difficult to register a small brain block without obvious anatomical outlines.
source: Though some frameworks can register certain types of brain slabs that contain complete coronal outlines slice by slice (Fürth et al., 2018; Song and Song, 2018; Ferrante and Paragios, 2017), it remains very difficult to register a small brain block without obvious anatomical outlines.
evidence: Stated in the introduction describing limitations of existing methods.

claim: Deep-learning-based brain mapping methods have been reported to directly provide segmentation/annotation of primary regions for 3D brain datasets.
source: As neural networks have emerged as a technique of choice for image processing (Long et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2018a; He et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019), deep-learning-based brain mapping methods have also recently been reported to directly provide segmentation/annotation of primary regions for 3D brain datasets (Iqbal et al., 2019; Akkus et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018b; Milletari et al., 2017; de Brebisson and Montana, 2015).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Deep-learning-based segmentation networks are efficient in extracting pixel-level features and are not dependent on the presence of global features such as complete anatomical outlines.
source: Such deep-learning-based segmentation networks are efficient in extracting pixel-level features and thus are not dependent on the presence of global features such as complete anatomical outlines, making them better suited for processing of incomplete brain data, as compared to registration-based methods.
evidence: Stated in the introduction describing advantages of deep learning methods.

claim: The establishment of deep learning networks relies on a sufficiently large training dataset, which is often laboriously registered, segmented, and annotated.
source: On the other hand, the establishment of these networks still relies on a sufficiently large training dataset, which is often laboriously registered, segmented, and annotated.
evidence: Stated in the introduction describing limitations of deep learning methods.

claim: A combination of image registration and a neural network can provide a synergistic improved analysis method and lead to more efficient and versatile brain mapping techniques.
source: Therefore, a combination of image registration and a neural network can possibly provide a synergistic improved analysis method and lead to more efficient and versatile brain mapping techniques.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as the rationale for the BIRDS approach.

claim: BIRDS was developed to allow investigators to quantify and spatially map 3D brain data in its own 3D digital space with reference to Allen CCFv3.
source: We developed BIRDS to allow investigators to quantify and spatially map 3D brain data in its own 3D digital space with reference to Allen CCFv3 (Wang et al., 2020b).
evidence: Stated in the introduction describing the purpose of BIRDS.

claim: The raw high-resolution 3D images obtained by STPT were first down-sampled into isotropic low-resolution data with a 20 μm voxel size identical to an averaged Allen template image.
source: The raw high-resolution 3D images (1 × 1 × 10 μm3 per voxel), obtained by serial two-photon tomography (STPT, see Materials and methods), were first down-sampled into isotropic low-resolution data with a 20 μm voxel size identical to an averaged Allen template image (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The re-sampling ratios along the x, y, and z axes were 0.05, 0.05 and 0.5, respectively.
source: The re-sampling ratios along the x (lateral-medial axis), y (dorsal-ventral axis), and z (anterior-posterior, AP axis) axes were thus 0.05, 0.05 and 0.5, respectively.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the preprocessing procedure.

claim: The preparation/mounting steps can cause non-uniform deformation of samples, thereby posing extra challenges to the precise registration of experimental image to an averaged template.
source: It should be noted that, in addition to the individual differences, the preparation/mounting steps can also cause non-uniform deformation of samples, thereby posing extra challenges to the precise registration of experimental image to an averaged template (Figure 1b, original dataset).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: A dynamic re-sampling ratio was applied to the z reslicing to mitigate the non-uniform deformation issue before registration.
source: To mitigate this non-uniform deformation issue before registration, we applied a dynamic re-sampling ratio rather than using a fixed value of 0.5 to the z reslicing.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the preprocessing method.

claim: The entire image stack was subdivided into multiple sub-stacks (n = 6) according to seven selected landmark planes.
source: We first subdivided the entire image stack into multiple sub-stacks (n = 6 in our demonstration, Figure 1a) according to seven selected landmark planes (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A dynamic z re-sampling ratio (varying from ~0.35 to 0.55) was applied to each sub-stack to better match the depth of each sub-stack to the Allen template brain.
source: Then we applied a dynamic z re-sampling ratio calculated corresponding to the positions of the landmark planes in the Allen template and sample data (varying from ~0.35 to 0.55) to each sub-stack, to finely compress (<0.5) or stretch (>0.5) the z depth of the sub-stacks, thereby better matching the depth of each sub-stack to the Allen template brain and rectifying the deformation along the AP axis (Figure 1a, Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The rectified whole-brain stack showed higher original similarity to the Allen template brain as compared to a raw experimental image stack.
source: The rectified whole-brain stack assembled by these dynamically re-sampled sub-stacks showed higher original similarity to the Allen template brain as compared to a raw experimental image stack (Figure 1b).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The implementation of the preprocessing step was beneficial for the better alignment of non-uniformly morphed brain data to a standardized template.
source: The implementation of such a preprocessing step was beneficial for the better alignment of non-uniformly morphed brain data to a standardized template (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Previous registration methods were vulnerable to inadequate alignment accuracy, which was associated with inadequate registration information provided by merely using the raw background image data.
source: We note that previous registration methods were vulnerable to inadequate alignment accuracy (Niedworok et al., 2016; Renier et al., 2016; Goubran et al., 2019), which was associated with inadequate registration information provided by merely using the raw background image data.
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: An assistant channel was generated to augment the image registration and enhance the accuracy.
source: To address this issue, in addition to the primary channel containing the background images of each sample and template brains, we further generated an assistant channel to augment the image registration and enhance the accuracy.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the bi-channel registration method.

claim: A phase congruency (PC) algorithm was used to extract the high-contrast edge and texture information from both the experimental and template brain images.
source: First, we used a phase congruency (PC) algorithm (Kovesi, 2019) to extract the high-contrast edge and texture information from both the experimental and template brain images based on their relatively fixed anatomy features (Figure 1c, Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citation and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: The geometry features of both brains along their lateral–medial, dorsal–ventral, and anterior–posterior axes were obtained with enhanced axial mutual information (MI) extracted using a grayscale reversal processing.
source: Then, we obtained the geometry features of both brains along their lateral–medial, dorsal–ventral, and anterior–posterior axes with enhanced axial mutual information (MI) extracted using a grayscale reversal processing (Maes et al., 1997; Thévenaz and Unser, 2000) (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citations and illustrated in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The bi-channel registration showed notably better registration accuracy as compared to conventional single-channel registration methods (aMAP, ClearMap, and MIRACL).
source: Finally, the primary channel containing raw brain images, in conjunction with the assistant channel containing the texture and geometry maps of brains, were included in the registration procedure to fulfill an information-augmented bi-channel registration requirement (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), which was verified to show notably better registration accuracy as compared to conventional single-channel registration methods (aMAP [Niedworok et al., 2016], ClearMap [Renier et al., 2016], and MIRACL [Goubran et al., 2019]).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citations and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: During registration, the MI gradually reached its maximum when the inverse grayscale images, PC images, and the raw images were finally geometrically aligned.
source: During registration, through an iterative optimization of the transformation from an averaged Allen brain template to the experimental data, the MI gradually reached its maximum when the inverse grayscale images, PC images, and the raw images were finally geometrically aligned (Figure 1d).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: The geometry wrapping parameters obtained from the registration process were applied to the Allen annotation file to generate a transformed version specifically for experimental data.
source: The geometry wrapping parameters obtained from the registration process were then applied to the Allen annotation file to generate a transformed version specifically for experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The dual-channel registration achieved fully automated registration/annotation at sufficiently high accuracy when processing STPT experimental data of an intact brain.
source: Our dual-channel registration achieved fully automated registration/annotation at sufficiently high accuracy when processing STPT experimental data of an intact brain (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citation supporting the claim.

claim: For low-quality or highly deformed brain data, the registration accuracy of the BIRDS method was reduced but still surpassed other methods.
source: As for low-quality or highly deformed brain data (e.g., clarified brain with obvious shrinkage), though the registration accuracy of our method was accordingly reduced, our method still quite obviously surpassed other methods (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: An interactive GUI was developed to permit manual correction of visible inaccuracies in the annotation file for challenging data types.
source: For such challenging data types, we also developed an interactive graphic user interface (GUI) to readily permit manual correction of the visible inaccuracies in the annotation file, through finely tuning the selected corresponding points (Figure 1e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1e.

claim: An accurate 3D annotation could be generated and applied to experimental data, either fully automatically (STPT data) or after mild manual correction (LSFM data of clarified brain).
source: Finally, an accurate 3D annotation could be generated and applied to experimental data, either fully automatically (STPT data) or after mild manual correction (light-sheet ﬂuorescence microscopy [LSFM] data of clarified brain), as shown in Figure 1f.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1f.

claim: The Allen annotation files transformed and registered by BIRDS were far better aligned with both STPT and LSFM images compared to aMAP, ClearMap, and MIRACL.
source: It was visually obvious that, as compared to the other three methods (green: aMAP; red: ClearMap; and blue: MIRACL in Figure 2a,b), the Allen annotation files transformed and registered by our BIRDS method (yellow in Figure 2a,b) were far better aligned with both STPT (as shown in VISC, CENT, AL, and PAL regions, Figure 2a) and LSFM (as shown in HPF, CB, VIS, and COA regions, Figure 2b) images.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2a,b.

claim: The median error distance (MED) obtained using BIRDS for STPT data was below 100 μm (~80 μm, n = 2).
source: In two different sets of STPT data, only our BIRDS method could provide an MED below 100 μm (~80 μm, n = 2), and this value slightly increased to ~120 μm for LSFM data (n = 3), but was still smaller than all the results obtained using the other three methods (aMAP, ~342 μm, n = 3; ClearMap, ~258 μm, n = 3; and MIRACL, ~175 μm, n = 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quantitative comparison results.

claim: The MED obtained using BIRDS for LSFM data was ~120 μm (n = 3).
source: In two different sets of STPT data, only our BIRDS method could provide an MED below 100 μm (~80 μm, n = 2), and this value slightly increased to ~120 μm for LSFM data (n = 3), but was still smaller than all the results obtained using the other three methods (aMAP, ~342 μm, n = 3; ClearMap, ~258 μm, n = 3; and MIRACL, ~175 μm, n = 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quantitative comparison results.

claim: The MED obtained using aMAP for LSFM data was ~342 μm (n = 3).
source: In two different sets of STPT data, only our BIRDS method could provide an MED below 100 μm (~80 μm, n = 2), and this value slightly increased to ~120 μm for LSFM data (n = 3), but was still smaller than all the results obtained using the other three methods (aMAP, ~342 μm, n = 3; ClearMap, ~258 μm, n = 3; and MIRACL, ~175 μm, n = 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quantitative comparison results.

claim: The MED obtained using ClearMap for LSFM data was ~258 μm (n = 3).
source: In two different sets of STPT data, only our BIRDS method could provide an MED below 100 μm (~80 μm, n = 2), and this value slightly increased to ~120 μm for LSFM data (n = 3), but was still smaller than all the results obtained using the other three methods (aMAP, ~342 μm, n = 3; ClearMap, ~258 μm, n = 3; and MIRACL, ~175 μm, n = 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quantitative comparison results.

claim: The MED obtained using MIRACL for LSFM data was ~175 μm (n = 3).
source: In two different sets of STPT data, only our BIRDS method could provide an MED below 100 μm (~80 μm, n = 2), and this value slightly increased to ~120 μm for LSFM data (n = 3), but was still smaller than all the results obtained using the other three methods (aMAP, ~342 μm, n = 3; ClearMap, ~258 μm, n = 3; and MIRACL, ~175 μm, n = 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quantitative comparison results.

claim: The highest Dice scores with an average median value of >0.89 (calculated for five brains) were obtained by BIRDS.
source: The highest Dice scores with an average median value of >0.89 (Supplementary file 3, calculated for five brains, 0.75, 0.81, and 0.81 for aMAP, ClearMap, and MIRACL) or >0.88 (Supplementary file 3, calculated using nine regions, 0.74, 0.77, and 0.84 for aMAP, ClearMap, and MIRACL, respectively) were obtained by BIRDS, further confirming the superior registration accuracy of our method.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quantitative comparison results.

claim: The average median Dice score calculated using nine regions for BIRDS was >0.88.
source: The highest Dice scores with an average median value of >0.89 (Supplementary file 3, calculated for five brains, 0.75, 0.81, and 0.81 for aMAP, ClearMap, and MIRACL) or >0.88 (Supplementary file 3, calculated using nine regions, 0.74, 0.77, and 0.84 for aMAP, ClearMap, and MIRACL, respectively) were obtained by BIRDS, further confirming the superior registration accuracy of our method.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quantitative comparison results.

claim: Through a comparative Wilcoxon test, BIRDS results were demonstrated to be superior to the other three methods with a p value < 0.05.
source: Through a comparative Wilcoxon test, our results were demonstrated to be superior to the other three methods (providing larger Dice scores) with a p value < 0.05 calculated either by brain or by region.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing statistical comparison results.

claim: A 3D digital map (CCFv3) based on the bi-channel registration was generated to support automatic annotation, analysis, and visualization of neurons in a whole mouse brain.
source: A 3D digital map (CCFv3) based on the abovementioned bi-channel registration was generated to support automatic annotation, analysis, and visualization of neurons in a whole mouse brain (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the digital map generation.

claim: The framework enabled large-scale mapping of neuronal connectivity and activity to reveal the architecture and function of brain circuits.
source: The framework thus enabled large-scale mapping of neuronal connectivity and activity to reveal the architecture and function of brain circuits.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the capabilities of the framework.

claim: A mouse brain containing six GFP-labeled layer-2/3 neurons in the right visual cortex was imaged with STPT at 1 × 1 × 10 μm3 resolution.
source: A mouse brain containing six GFP-labeled layer-2/3 neurons in the right visual cortex was imaged with STPT at 1 × 1 × 10 μm3 resolution (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citation describing the experimental data.

claim: An interactive hierarchal tree of brain regions in the software interface allowed navigation through the corresponding selected-and-highlighted brain regions with its annotation information.
source: An interactive hierarchal tree of brain regions in the software interface allowed navigation through the corresponding selected-and-highlighted brain regions with its annotation information (Figure 3b, Video 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3b and Video 1.

claim: Through linking with Imaris, each fluorescently labeled neuronal cell (n = 5) was visualized and traced using the filament module of Imaris across the 3D space of the entire brain.
source: Through linking with Imaris, we visualized and traced each fluorescently labeled neuronal cell (n = 5) using the filament module of Imaris across the 3D space of the entire brain (Figure 3c, Materials and methods, Video 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3c and Video 2.

claim: BIRDS can apply reverse transformation to a raw image stack to generate a standard template-like rendered 3D map, including both traced axonal projections and selected whole-brain structures.
source: The BIRD software can also apply reverse transformation to a raw image stack to generate a standard template-like rendered 3D map, including both traced axonal projections and selected whole-brain structures, which faithfully captures true 3D axonal arborization patterns and anatomical locations, as shown in Figure 3d.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3d.

claim: BIRDS can quantify the lengths and arborizations of traced axons according to the segmentation of the 3D digital map.
source: This software can also quantify the lengths and arborizations of traced axons according to the segmentation of the 3D digital map generated using the BIRDS pipeline (Figure 3e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3e.

claim: BIRDS can be linked to Imaris to perform automated cell counting with higher efficiency and accuracy.
source: BIRDS can be linked to Imaris to perform automated cell counting with higher efficiency and accuracy (Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the cell counting capability.

claim: Neurons were retrogradely labeled by CAV-mCherry injected to the right striatum and imaged by STPT at 1×1×10 μm3 resolution.
source: Here, we demonstrate it with an example brain where neurons were retrogradely labeled by CAV-mCherry injected to the right striatum and imaged by STPT at 1×1×10 μm3 resolution (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with citation describing the experimental data.

claim: Imaris calculated the local image statistics for cell recognition only using the image stack within each segregated area, thereby fitting the dynamic range of the local images to achieve better results.
source: Imaris calculated the local image statistics for cell recognition only using the image stack within each segregated area; therefore, it fit the dynamic range of the local images to achieve better results, as shown in the middle column in the right panel of Figure 4a.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: The conventional Imaris automated cell counting program processed the whole-brain image stack at once to calculate the global cell recognition parameters for every brain area, which easily resulted in false positive or false negative counts in brain areas where the labeling signal was too strong or too weak compared to the global signal.
source: In contrast, the conventional Imaris automated cell counting program processed the whole-brain image stack at once to calculate the global cell recognition parameters for every brain area, which easily resulted in false positive or false negative counts in brain areas where the labeling signal was too strong or too weak compared to the global signal, as demonstrated in the STR and SB in the right column of the right panels of Figure 4a, respectively.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: Compared to conventional Imaris results, BIRDS–Imaris results were more consistent with manual cell counting, especially for brain regions where the fluorescent signal was at the high or low end of the dynamic range.
source: Compared to conventional Imaris results, our BIRDS–Imaris results were more consistent with a manual one, especially for brain regions where the fluorescent signal was at the high or low end of the dynamic range (BS and STR, Figure 4e).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4e.

claim: BIRDS–Imaris can process each segmented brain area separately, calculating the parameters for the cell recognition algorithm using local image statistics instead of processing the whole-brain image stack at once.
source: Thanks to the 3D digital map generated by the BIRDS pipeline, BIRDS–Imaris can process each segmented brain area separately, namely calculating the parameters for the cell recognition algorithm using local image statistics instead of processing the whole-brain image stack at once.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the advantage of BIRDS–Imaris.

claim: The segmented cell counting strategy is much less demanding on computation resources and is optimized for each brain area to solve the problem that the same globe cell recognition parameter works poorly in certain brain regions with signal intensity at either of the two extreme ends of the dynamic range of the entire brain.
source: Such a segmented cell counting strategy is much less demanding on computation resources, and moreover, it is optimized for each brain area to solve the problem that the same globe cell recognition parameter works poorly in certain brain regions with signal intensity at either of the two extreme ends of the dynamic range of the entire brain.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the advantages of the segmented cell counting strategy.

claim: A deep neural network (DNN)-based method was introduced for efficient segmentation/annotation of incomplete brain sections with minimal human supervision.
source: To overcome this limitation, we further introduced a deep neural network (DNN)-based method for efficient segmentation/annotation of incomplete brain sections with minimal human supervision.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the DNN-based method.

claim: A Deeplab V3+ network based on an encoding-decoding structure was optimized for the deep-learning implementation.
source: Herein, we optimized a Deeplab V3+ network, which was based on an encoding-decoding structure, for our deep-learning implementation (Figure 5a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5a.

claim: The training of a neural network fundamentally requires a sufficiently large dataset containing various incomplete brain blocks which have been well segmented.
source: It should be noted that the training of a neural network fundamentally requires a sufficiently large dataset containing various incomplete brain blocks which have been well segmented.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the requirements for DNN training.

claim: The efficient BIRDS method could readily obtain a large number of labeled datasets through cropping processed whole brains without experiencing time-consuming manual annotation.
source: Benefiting from our efficient BIRDS method, we could readily obtain a large number of such labeled datasets through cropping processed whole brains and without experiencing time-consuming manual annotation.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the advantage of BIRDS for generating training data.

claim: Various types of incomplete brains were generated and sent to the DNN for iterative training, after which the skilled network could directly infer the segmentations/annotations for new modes of incomplete brain images.
source: Various types of incomplete brains, as shown in Figure 5b, were hereby generated and sent to our DNN for iterative training, after which the skilled network could directly infer the segmentations/annotations for new modes of incomplete brain images (Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5b.

claim: The DNN successfully inferred annotation results for a cropped hemisphere, irregular cut of hemisphere, and a randomly cropped volume.
source: Next, we validated the network performance on three different modes of input brain images cropped from the registered whole-brain dataset (STPT). The DNN successfully inferred annotation results for a cropped hemisphere, irregular cut of hemisphere, and a randomly cropped volume, as shown in Figure 5c–e, respectively.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5c–e.

claim: The inferred annotations were found to be highly similar to the registered annotation results in all three types of incomplete data.
source: The inferred annotations (red lines) were found to be highly similar to the registered annotation results (green lines) in all three types of incomplete data.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the validation results.

claim: The averaged median Dice scores for the individual sub-regions in the hemisphere, irregular cut of hemisphere, and random volumes were 0.86, 0.87, and 0.87, respectively.
source: The averaged median Dice scores for the individual sub-regions in the hemisphere, irregular cut of hemisphere, and random volumes were 0.86, 0.87, and 0.87, respectively, showing a sufficiently high inference accuracy in most of brain regions, such as the isocortex, HPF, OLF, or STR.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the quantitative validation results.

claim: The performance of the network for segmentation using PAL, MBsta, P-sen regions remained sub-optimal (Dice score 0.78–0.8), due to their lack of obvious borders, and large structural variations across planes.
source: It is worth noting that the performance of our network for segmentation using PAL, MBsta, P-sen regions remained sub-optimal (Dice score 0.78–0.8), due to their lack of obvious borders, and large structural variations across planes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The network was applied to generate 3D atlases for three incomplete brains, segmenting the hemisphere into 18 regions, the irregular cut of half the telencephalon into 10 regions, and the random volume into seven regions.
source: Finally, we applied our network inferences to generate 3D atlases for these three incomplete brains, while segmenting the hemisphere into 18 regions such as the Isocortex, HPF, OLF, CTXsp, STR, PAL, CB, DORpm, DORsm, HY, MBsen, MBmot, MBsta, P-sen, P-mot, P-sat, MY-sen, and MY-mot, while we processed an irregular cut of half the telencephalon into 10 regions as Isocortex, HPF, OLF, CTXsp, STR, PAL, DORpm, DORsm, and HY, MY-mot, and the random volume into seven regions, defined as the Isocortex, HPF, STR, PAL, DORpm, DORsm, and HY (Figure 5f,g,h).
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5f,g,h.

claim: The DNN performed reasonably well even if the brain was highly incomplete.
source: Therefore, our DNN performed reasonably well even if the brain was highly incomplete.
evidence: Stated in the Results section summarizing the DNN performance.

claim: The DNN could achieve second-level fine segmentation within a small brain region of interest, such as successfully segmenting the hippocampus (CA1, CA2, CA3, and DG).
source: Furthermore, it could achieve second-level fine segmentation within a small brain region of interest. For example, we successfully segmented the hippocampus (CA1, CA2, CA3, and DG), as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.
evidence: Stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The unique capability of the DNN was possibly derived from the detection of pixel-level features rather than regions, thereby substantially strengthening the robustness of the hybrid BIRDS method over conventional brain registration techniques when the data is highly incomplete/defective.
source: Such a unique capability of our DNN was possibly derived from the detection of pixel-level features rather than regions, and thereby substantially strengthened the robustness of our hybrid BIRDS method over conventional brain registration techniques when the data is highly incomplete/defective.
evidence: Stated in the Results section explaining the advantage of the DNN approach.

claim: The bi-channel image registration method, in conjunction with a deep-learning framework, readily provides accuracy-improved anatomical segmentation for whole mouse brain in reference to an Allen average template.
source: In summary, we demonstrate a bi-channel image registration method, in conjunction with a deep-learning framework, to readily provide accuracy-improved anatomical segmentation for whole mouse brain in reference to an Allen average template, and direct segmentation inference for incomplete brain datasets, which were otherwise not easily registered to standardized whole-brain space.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion summarizing the main contribution.

claim: The addition of a brain feature channel to the registration process greatly improved the accuracy of automatically registering individual whole-brain data with a standardized Allen average template.
source: The addition of a brain feature channel to the registration process greatly improved the accuracy of automatically registering individual whole-brain data with a standardized Allen average template.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion summarizing the key finding.

claim: The registration is currently limited to using on like-imaged brains, such as brains imaged using wide-field, confocal, or light-sheet microscopes, because it is based on two-photon template images provided by Allen CCF.
source: It should be noted that the registration was based on two-photon template images provided by Allen CCF, so it is currently limited to using on like-imaged brains, for example, brains imaged using wide-field, confocal, or light-sheet microscopes, etc.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion describing a limitation of the method.

claim: The deep neural network was applied to rapidly infer segmentations for various incomplete brain datasets, which were challenging for registration-based methods while remaining very common in neuroscience research.
source: For processing various incomplete brain datasets, which were challenging for registration-based methods while remaining very common in neuroscience research, we applied our deep neural network to rapidly infer segmentations.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion describing the application of the DNN.

claim: A full annotation using a neural network is currently too computationally demanding as compared to registration-based segmentation.
source: Though a full annotation using a neural network is currently too computationally demanding as compared to registration-based segmentation, it is undoubtedly a good complement to registration-based segmentation.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion comparing the computational demands of the two approaches.

claim: In the hybrid BIRDS pipeline, the DNN inference greatly reinforced the inefficient side of registration, while the registration also readily provided high-quality training data for the DNN.
source: Therefore, in our hybrid BIRDS pipeline, the DNN inference greatly reinforced the inefficient side of registration, while the registration also readily provided high-quality training data for our DNN.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion describing the synergistic relationship.

claim: The synergistic effect in the BIRDS method could provide a paradigm shift for enabling robust and efficient 3D image segmentation/annotation for biology research.
source: We believe such a synergistic effect in our method could provide a paradigm shift for enabling robust and efficient 3D image segmentation/annotation for biology research.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a belief about the impact of the method.

claim: Network-based segmentation will play an increasingly important role in new pipelines with the unceasing development of deep learning.
source: With the unceasing development of deep learning, we envision that network-based segmentation will play an increasingly important role in new pipelines.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a prediction about future developments.

claim: A variety of applications, such as tracing of long-distance neuronal projections and parallel counting of cell populations in different brain regions, was enabled as a result of the efficient brain mapping.
source: A variety of applications, such as tracing of long-distance neuronal projections and parallel counting of cell populations in different brain regions, was also enabled as a result of our efficient brain mapping.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion describing the applications enabled by BIRDS.

claim: The BIRDS pipeline is now fully open source and has been packaged into a Fiji plugin to facilitate biological researchers.
source: The BIRDS pipeline is now fully open source and also has been packaged into a Fiji plugin to facilitate biological researchers.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion describing the availability of the software.

claim: The BIRDS method can immediately allow new insights using current brain mapping techniques, and thus further push the resolution and scale limits in future explorations of brain space.
source: We sincerely expect that the BIRDS method can immediately allow new insights using current brain mapping techniques, and thus further push the resolution and scale limits in future explorations of brain space.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an expectation about the impact of the method.

claim: Brains 1 and 2 were obtained with STPT, and each dataset encompassed ~180 Gigavoxels.
source: Brains 1 and 2 were obtained with STPT, and each dataset encompassed ~180 Gigavoxels, for example, 11,980 × 7540 × 1075 in Dataset 1, with a voxel size of 1 × 1 × 10 μm3.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the STPT data.

claim: Individual neuronal axons were labeled with plasmid DNA (pCAG-eGFP) by two-photon microscopy-guided single-cell electroporation.
source: Individuals neuronal axons were labeled with plasmid DNA (pCAG-eGFP [Addgene accession 11150]) by two-photon microscopy-guided single-cell electroporation, and the brain was fixed by cardioperfusion of 4% paraformaldehyde 8 days later.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the labeling procedure.

claim: Striatum-projecting neurons were labeled by stereotactically injecting PRV-cre into the right striatum of tdTomato reporter mice (Ai14, JAX).
source: Striatum-projecting neurons were labeled by stereotactically injecting PRV-cre into the right striatum of tdTomato reporter mice (Ai14, JAX), and the brain was fixed cardioperfusion 30 days later.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the labeling procedure.

claim: The brains were embedded in 5% oxidized agarose and imaged with a commercial STPT (TissueVision, USA) excited at 940 nm.
source: The brains were embedded in 5% oxidized agarose and imaged with a commercial STPT (TissueVision, USA) excited at 940 nm.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the imaging procedure.

claim: Coronally, the brain was optically scanned every 10 μm at 1 μm/pixel without averaging and physically sectioned every 50 μm.
source: Coronally, the brain was optically scanned every 10 μm at 1 μm/pixel without averaging and physically sectioned every 50 μm.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the imaging parameters.

claim: Brains 3, 4, and 5 were obtained with LSFM and each dataset encompassed ~700 Gigavoxels (~10,000 × 8000 × 5000), with an isotropic voxel size of 1 μm3.
source: Brains 3, 4, and 5 were obtained with LSFM and each dataset encompassed ~700 Gigavoxels (~10,000 × 8000 × 5000), with an isotropic voxel size of 1 μm3.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the LSFM data.

claim: Brain tissues of eight-week-old Thy-GFP-M mice were first clarified with u-DISCO protocol before imaging.
source: Brain tissues of eight-week-old Thy-GFP-M mice (RRID:IMSR_JAX:007788) were first clarified with u-DISCO protocol (Pan et al., 2016) before imaging.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with citation describing the sample preparation.

claim: Brains 3 and 4 were acquired using a custom-built Bessel plane illumination microscope, a type of LSFM modality employing non-diffraction thin Bessel light-sheet.
source: Brains 3 and 4 were acquired using a custom-built Bessel plane illumination microscope, a type of LSFM modality employing non-diffraction thin Bessel light-sheet.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the imaging modality.

claim: Brain 5 was whole-brain 3D image of a Thy-GFP-M mice acquired using a lab-built selective plane illumination microscope, another LSFM modality combining Gaussian light-sheet with multi-view image acquisition/fusion.
source: Brain 5 was whole-brain 3D image of a Thy-GFP-M mice acquired using a lab-built selective plane illumination microscope (Nie et al., 2020), another LSFM modality combining Gaussian light-sheet with multi-view image acquisition/fusion.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with citation describing the imaging modality.

claim: An interactive GUI was developed in the Fiji plugin to correspond the coronal planes in the Allen Reference Atlas (132 planes, 100 μm interval) with those in the experimental 3D image stack.
source: First, we developed an interactive GUI in the Fiji plugin (RRID:SCR_002285) to correspond the coronal planes in the Allen Reference Atlas (ARA) (132 planes, 100 μm interval) with those in the experimental 3D image stack (e.g., 1075 planes with 10 μm stepsize in Dataset 1).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the preprocessing implementation.

claim: The computational cost of the data re-sampling operation was low, taking merely ~5 min for processing 180 GB raw STPT data on a Xeon workstation (E5-2630 V3 CPU).
source: The computational cost of abovementioned data re-sampling operation was low, taking merely ~5 min for processing 180 GB raw STPT data on a Xeon workstation (E5-2630 V3 CPU).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the computational performance.

claim: The bi-channel registration procedure is implemented based on the Elastix open-source program (Version 4.9.0).
source: Our bi-channel registration procedure is implemented based on the Elastix open-source program (Version 4.9.0) (Shamonin et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with citations describing the implementation.

claim: Rigid+affine+B-spline three-level model was used for the registration, with rigid and affine transformations mainly for aligning the overall orientation differences between the datasets, and B-spline model mainly for aligning the local geometry differences.
source: Here we used rigid+affine+B-spline three-level model for the registration, with rigid and affine transformations mainly for aligning the overall orientation differences between the datasets, and B-spline model mainly for aligning the local geometry differences.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the registration model.

claim: A stepsize of 30 pixels was set for the movement of control points in 3D space, and a five-level coarse-to-fine pyramidal registration was applied for achieving faster convergence.
source: A stepsize of 30 pixels was set for the movement of control points in 3D space, and a five-level coarse-to-fine pyramidal registration was applied for achieving faster convergence.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the registration parameters.

claim: A Marching cubes algorithm was introduced to generate 3D surface graphics for the 3D digital map.
source: In order to generate a digital frame for quantitative analysis, we introduced Marching cubes algorithm (Lorensen and Cline, 1987) to generate 3D surface graphics, which is also, to generate the 3D digital maps.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with citation describing the visualization method.

claim: Through the programmable API link with Imaris, the 3D digital map could be readily visualized and various quantification could be performed in Imaris.
source: Then, through the programmable API link with Imaris (RRID:SCR_007370), we could readily visualize the 3D digital map and perform various quantification in Imaris.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the visualization and quantification capability.

claim: Neuron tracing and cell counting tasks could be performed in Imaris at native resolution (e.g., 1 × 1 × 10 μm3 for STPT data).
source: After registration and interpolation applied to the experimental data, a 3D digital map was visualized in Imaris (9.0.0) invoked by our program. Then neuron tracing and cell counting tasks could be performed in Imaris at native resolution (e.g., 1 × 1 × 10 μm3 for STPT data).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the analysis capabilities.

claim: The cell counting could be performed in parallel by simultaneously setting a number of kernel diameters and intensity thresholds for different segmented brain regions.
source: Furthermore, the cell counting could be performed in parallel by simultaneously setting a number of kernel diameters and intensity thresholds for different segmented brain regions.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the cell counting procedure.

claim: Two skillful persons independently repeated the manual segmentation process for five times, and a STAPLE algorithm was used to fuse the 10 manual segmentation results to obtain the final averaged output as the ground-truth segmentation.
source: To allow the manual segmentation as objective as possible, two skillful persons independently repeated the abovementioned process for five times, and a STAPLE algorithm (Warfield et al., 2004) was used to fuse the 10 manual segmentation results to obtain the final averaged output as the ground-truth segmentation, for each region.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with citation describing the ground truth generation.

claim: Eighteen primary regions (levels 4 and 5) in whole brain were chosen for the DNN training and performance validation.
source: We chose 18 primary regions (levels 4 and 5): Isocortex, HPF, OLF, CTXsp, STR, PAL, CB, DORpm, DORsm, HY, MBsen, MBmot, Mbsta, P-sen, P-mot, P-sat, MY-sen, and MY-mot, in whole brain for the DNN training and performance validation.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the DNN training setup.

claim: Nine whole mouse brains containing 5000 annotated sagittal slices (660 × 400 for each slice) were used as the training dataset.
source: Nine whole mouse brains containing 5000 annotated sagittal slices (660 × 400 for each slice) were first used as the training dataset.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the training data.

claim: The training dataset was comprised of both complete and incomplete sagittal sections (5000 and 4500 slices, respectively).
source: The training dataset were thus comprised both complete and incomplete sagittal sections (5000 and 4500 slices, respectively).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the training data composition.

claim: The network was trained for ~30,000 iterations with a learning rate of 0.001, learning momentum of 0.9 and output stride of 8.
source: The network was trained for ~30,000 iterations with a learning rate of 0.001, learning momentum of 0.9 and output stride of 8.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the training parameters.

claim: The training was implemented using two NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080Ti graphics cards and took approximately 40 hr.
source: The training was implemented using two NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080Ti graphics cards and took approximately 40 hr.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the computational resources and time.

claim: BIRDS was run on a Windows 10 workstation equipped with dual Xeon E5-2630 V3 CPUs, 1 TB RAM, and two GeForce GTX 1080 Ti graphic cards.
source: We run BIRDS on a Windows 10 workstation equipped with dual Xeon E5-2630 V3 CPUs, 1 TB RAM, and two GeForce GTX 1080 Ti graphic cards.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the computing resources.

claim: Memory with capacity at least 1.5 times of the data size is required for generating the 3D digital framework.
source: It should be noted that memory with capacity at least 1.5 times of the data size is required at this step.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the memory requirements.

claim: When applying BIRDS to larger datasets, such as rat brain, a powerful workstation with at least one XEON CPU, 1 TB memory, and one state-of-the-art graphic card (Geforce RTX 3090) is recommended.
source: Therefore, when applying BIRDS to larger datasets, such as rat brain, we will recommend a powerful workstation with at least one XEON CPU, 1 TB memory, and one state-of-the-art graphic card (Geforce RTX 3090), to guarantee a smooth running of whole pipeline.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section as a recommendation for larger datasets.

claim: The source code of BIRDS for Windows 10 is available at https://github.com/bleach1by1/birds_reg.
source: We have provided source code of the BIRDS for Windows 10 at https://github.com/bleach1by1/birds_reg (Wang, 2021a; copy archived at swh:1:rev:22cf3d792c3887708a65ddae43d6dde7ed8b7836).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing code availability.

claim: FIJI plugin and ancillary installation packages are provided at https://github.com/bleach1by1/BIRDS_plugin.
source: FIJI plugin and ancillary installation packages are provided at https://github.com/bleach1by1/BIRDS_plugin (Wang, 2021b; copy archived at swh:1:rev:41e90d4518321d6ca8e806ccadb2809bfa6bd475).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing plugin availability.

claim: BIRDS contains five core modules: image preprocessing, bi-channel registration, manual correction, link with Imaris software, and deep-learning segmentation.
source: BIRDS contains five core modules, image preprocessing, bi-channel registration, manual correction, link with Imaris software, and deep-learning segmentation, all of which can be executed on a GUI.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the software modules.

claim: A step-by-step tutorial and test data were provided to facilitate the program implementation by other researchers.
source: We also provided a step-by-step tutorial and test data to facilitate the program implementation by other researchers.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section describing the documentation provided.
